keyVerseText: That Hadad fled, he and certain Edomites of his father's servants with him, to go into Egypt; Hadad being yet a little child.
rootMeaning: The root of אֲדַד (ʼĂdad) is likely related to חֲדַד (Chădad), which means "mighty" and is associated with a son of Ishmael. This connection suggests that אֲדַד carries connotations of strength and power. The etymological note that אֲדַד may be an orthographical variation of חֲדַד emphasizes its linguistic link to the idea of might, which adds depth beyond the simple proper name to imply a figure of significant influence or force.
usageInScripture: The word אֲדַד appears only once in Scripture, translated in 1 Kings 11:17 as "That Hadad," referring to an Edomite enemy raised up by God to punish Solomon. This singular occurrence highlights its specific identification as a proper name rather than a common noun. The consistency in translation underscores its role as a distinct historical figure connected to divine judgment rather than a general concept.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אֲדַד as a name tied to might and power enriches the theological narrative of God's sovereignty in using nations and individuals to accomplish His purposes. Hadad, as an Edomite adversary, exemplifies how God can raise up opponents to discipline His people for their unfaithfulness, demonstrating divine justice and holiness. This reminds believers that God’s control extends even over enemies, and that His judgments serve a redemptive purpose. Recognizing the meaning behind the name deepens our appreciation for the intricacies of God's providence and the seriousness of sin.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Kings 11:17, the phrase "That Hadad fled, he and certain Edomites of his father's servants with him, to go into Egypt; Hadad being yet a little child" introduces Hadad as a significant figure whose early flight sets the stage for his later role as an adversary to Solomon. The name אֲדַד here not only identifies this individual but also hints at the power and threat he would embody. This verse situates Hadad within God's sovereign plan to bring consequences for Solomon’s sins, emphasizing the personal and historical dimensions of divine discipline.
